title: Eiffel Tower with Trees

image.credit: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York; via arthistoryproject.com

altText: The Eiffel Tower in Paris painted in broken, tilting pieces, with trees in the foreground. The tower looks as if it is sliding and bending rather than standing straight.

source.museum: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York
source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, year, medium, collection, public-domain statement)

context: An oil painting by Robert Delaunay, a French artist, made in 1910. Its French title is Tour Eiffel aux arbres. Delaunay painted the Eiffel Tower many times, and here the famous Paris landmark is treated as a subject to take apart and rebuild in paint.

descriptions.k: This is a very tall tower in a big city. It is the Eiffel Tower. The painter made it look wobbly and broken into pieces. Trees are in front. Can you find the tower? Does it look like it is dancing?
descriptions.g12: Robert Delaunay painted the Eiffel Tower in Paris, France. But it does not look like a photograph. The tower seems to tilt and break into pieces, and trees stand in front. What shapes can you find, and does the tower feel strong or shaky?
descriptions.g35: Robert Delaunay painted Eiffel Tower with Trees in 1910 in France. The tower was a new landmark in Paris then. Delaunay did not paint it as a neat, straight building. He broke it into tilting pieces and placed trees in front. Why might an artist show a famous place in this surprising way? Look for details that support your idea.
descriptions.g68: In Eiffel Tower with Trees (1910), Robert Delaunay paints the Paris landmark as fractured, leaning forms instead of a stable structure. Trees in front add another layer. The tower was a symbol of modern engineering, and the broken, shifting view makes it feel active. What do you think the artist wanted to show about modern city life, and how does the composition support that?
descriptions.g910: Delaunay's Eiffel Tower with Trees (1910) fragments a famous symbol of modern Paris into tilting, overlapping planes. The approach shows the influence of Cubist ideas about seeing from several points at once, but Delaunay emphasized movement and color. How does the shattered tower change what the monument means, and how do the trees alter the balance between nature and the modern city?
descriptions.g1112: Eiffel Tower with Trees (1910) belongs to Delaunay's series on the Eiffel Tower, in which the monument of modern engineering is fractured and set in motion. Its debt to Cubist fragmentation sits alongside his own interest in color and rhythm, which later led toward abstraction. Does the painting celebrate modernity, question its stability, or both? What visual evidence supports your reading?

k.daily: Can you find the tall tower? What is it doing in this picture?
k.emotion: Does the tower feel happy, scary, or exciting to you? What makes you say that?
k.observation: Find the trees. Where are they compared with the tower?
k.analysis: What shapes do you see that look like broken pieces?
k.line: Trace one slanted line from the tower with your finger. Which way does it lean?
k.shape: What triangle or pointy shapes can you find in the tower?
k.color: Which colors did the painter use for the tower? Are they bright or dull?
k.texture: Does the picture feel smooth or choppy? Tell us what you see.
k.space: Is the tower far away or close up? How can you tell?
k.light: Which parts of the picture look bright and which look dark?
k.meaning: Why might a painter want to paint a tall famous tower?
k.culture: What famous place near your home would you like to paint?
k.technique: How might the painter have used paint to make the tower look like it is moving?
k.personal: If you could stand beside this tower, what would you hear?
k.critical: What would you change in this picture to make the tower look more like a photo?

g12.daily: How can you tell that the painter wanted this Eiffel Tower to feel like it is moving?
g12.emotion: Does the painting feel calm or energetic? Point to the parts that show it.
g12.observation: Name five different things you can see in the tower area of the painting.
g12.analysis: Why do the trees in front make the tower feel farther back?
g12.line: Follow the slanting lines of the tower. Where do they lead your eye?
g12.shape: How do the pointy shapes of the tower differ from the shapes of the trees?
g12.color: Which colors repeat in the tower and the trees, and how do they make the painting feel connected?
g12.texture: How do the broken patches of paint make the picture feel choppy or bumpy?
g12.space: How does the painter show that the tower is tall and the trees are closer?
g12.light: Where do you see bright patches, and how do they help the tower stand out?
g12.meaning: Why might a tower of iron be a good subject for a painter in 1910?
g12.culture: How might a visitor to Paris in 1910 have felt about seeing this tower?
g12.technique: How can you tell that the painter did not copy the tower exactly?
g12.personal: What would you notice if you painted a tall building near your home from far away and then up close?
g12.critical: Which part of the painting is the hardest to figure out? What makes it tricky?

g35.daily: Where do you see the greatest difference between this painting and a photograph of the Eiffel Tower?
g35.emotion: How would you describe the energy of this painting, and which details create it?
g35.observation: Look at the tower closely. Which pieces look broken or tilted?
g35.analysis: How do the trees in front change the way you see the tower behind them?
g35.line: How do the slanting lines of the tower create a feeling of movement?
g35.shape: How do the triangular shapes in the tower compare with the rounder shapes of the trees?
g35.color: How do earthy and bright colors work together to hold the broken tower together?
g35.texture: How does the choppy painting surface give a feeling of motion instead of stillness?
g35.space: How does Delaunay mix near and far so that the tower seems to rise above the trees?
g35.light: How do light patches help your eye find the tower's tall frame?
g35.meaning: In 1910 the Eiffel Tower was a symbol of new technology. How might Delaunay's painting show excitement or worry about change?
g35.culture: What might people in Paris around 1910 have thought about a landmark like this being shown in pieces?
g35.technique: What clues show that Delaunay rebuilt the tower from many views rather than one?
g35.personal: What landmark near you would you break into pieces in a painting, and why?
g35.critical: Does the tower have to look realistic for the painting to feel true? Explain using what you see.

g68.daily: What does Delaunay's broken, tilting tower suggest about how he saw modern Paris?
g68.emotion: What mood does the painting have, and how do its shapes and colors create it?
g68.observation: What stands out when you compare the tower with the trees in front of it?
g68.analysis: How does the layering of trees and tower shape how your eye moves through the painting?
g68.line: How do the diagonal lines of the tower create energy, and where do they meet?
g68.shape: How do sharp, angular shapes in the tower contrast with the softer shapes of the foliage?
g68.color: How does Delaunay's color help unite the fractured forms of the tower and the trees?
g68.texture: How does the visible, broken surface suggest motion rather than a calm, finished view?
g68.space: How does Delaunay create depth when he also flattens and tilts the shapes?
g68.light: How do contrasts of light and dark help define the structure of the tower?
g68.meaning: What might it mean to depict a symbol of modern engineering as unstable and shifting?
g68.culture: How might the Eiffel Tower's role as a symbol of Paris affect how people read this painting?
g68.technique: How does breaking an object into many viewpoints change the way a painting is made?
g68.personal: How does the painting change how you think about a familiar landmark in your own life?
g68.critical: Is this painting more a celebration or a critique of the modern city? Argue with visual evidence.

g910.daily: How does Delaunay's fragmentation of the Eiffel Tower change its meaning from a monument to an experience?
g910.emotion: What emotional tone emerges from the tilting planes and the muted, earthy palette?
g910.observation: Study the places where the tower breaks apart. What do these breaks imply about the way the artist observed?
g910.analysis: How does the overlap of trees and tower establish a hierarchy of foreground and landmark?
g910.line: How do diagonals and repeated slanted lines build rhythm across the composition?
g910.shape: How do the geometric, angular structures contrast with the organic shapes of the trees?
g910.color: How does color, rather than line alone, hold the shattered forms together?
g910.texture: What does the broken brushwork communicate about movement and about the artist's process?
g910.space: How does the composition deny a single, stable viewpoint, and what does that imply about perception?
g910.light: How does the alternation of light and shadow fragment the tower while still suggesting its structure?
g910.meaning: What might the tower, as a symbol of modernity, represent when shown as unsteady?
g910.culture: How does the work reflect the wider artistic experimentation in France in the early 1900s?
g910.technique: How does the influence of Cubist ideas show in Delaunay's approach, and where does he depart from it?
g910.personal: How does this image challenge your assumption that a painting should show a place as it looks to a camera?
g910.critical: How would you judge whether this painting still honors the tower it depicts, or transforms it into something new?

g1112.daily: How does Delaunay's treatment of the Eiffel Tower reframe a monument of modern engineering as a site of perceptual and cultural instability?
g1112.emotion: How does the painting's mood arise from fractured planes and a restrained, earthy palette, and how might viewers differ in feeling it?
g1112.observation: Examine where the structure of the tower dissolves. Do these breaks read as damage, motion, or multiple viewpoints?
g1112.analysis: How does the layered placement of trees and tower organize spatial relationships?
g1112.line: How do the repeated diagonals generate rhythm and a sense of vertigo in the composition?
g1112.shape: How does the tension between geometric tower and organic trees complicate the opposition of nature and the modern city?
g1112.color: How does the color structure hold the fragmented forms together, and how does it anticipate Delaunay's later move toward abstraction?
g1112.texture: What does the broken, constructive surface suggest about the relationship between seeing and painting?
g1112.space: How does the denial of a fixed vantage point work as an argument about perception rather than a depiction of a view?
g1112.light: How does the interplay of light and shadow reinforce the fragmentation while preserving a sense of the tower's identity?
g1112.meaning: What competing interpretations of the shaken tower, celebration of modernity or anxiety about it, does the painting support?
g1112.culture: How does the Eiffel Tower's status as a Paris symbol affect the stakes of Delaunay's experiment?
g1112.technique: How does Delaunay adapt Cubist fragmentation to his own interest in color and movement?
g1112.personal: How does viewing the painting shift your sense of what it means to know a place by sight?
g1112.critical: What criteria would you use to defend this painting to a viewer who wants a faithful picture of the tower?

teacherNote.context: A 1910 oil painting by Robert Delaunay of the Eiffel Tower, in his series on the monument. The collection was completed from general knowledge because the source page text is cut off.
directions: Have students sketch a local landmark from two positions and combine the views into one drawing.
Compare this with a photograph of the Eiffel Tower and list what each shows that the other cannot.
Discuss why artists in the early 1900s were drawn to engineering structures as subjects.
